subject: English
topic: Fill in the Blanks — Advanced Grammar and Vocabulary (W11 B2)

questions.stem: Neither the manager nor the employees ______ aware of the new regulation.
questions.explanation: B is correct. With 'Neither...nor', the verb agrees with the subject closest to it (the nearer subject rule). 'Employees' (plural) is closer to the verb. Therefore use 'were'. Rule: Neither X nor Y → verb agrees with Y. If Y is plural → plural verb. Trap: 'was' = wrong (would apply if the singular subject 'manager' were closer); 'is/are being' = present tense is wrong for a past situation implied by 'aware of the new regulation' requiring a simple state verb.

questions.stem: He has been working in this company ______ five years.
questions.explanation: C is correct. FOR + duration (a period of time): 'for five years' = a span of time. SINCE + point in time: 'since 2019' = a specific time marker. 'Five years' is a duration, so FOR is correct. Trap: Since = correct with a specific starting point like 'since 2019', not a duration like 'five years'; During = used with named periods like 'during the meeting'.

questions.stem: The committee ______ reached a unanimous decision after three hours of deliberation.
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'The committee' is a collective noun. In standard British/SSC English, collective nouns are treated as singular when acting as a single unit: 'The committee has decided' (acting together). The Present Perfect singular 'has reached' is correct. Trap: 'have reached' = used when committee members are acting individually (not as a unit); 'were' = wrong tense and number; 'had been' = Past Perfect (no context for a prior past action).

questions.stem: She speaks English ______ her mother tongue.
questions.explanation: B is correct. LIKE (preposition) = comparing nouns/pronouns. 'She speaks English like her mother tongue' = comparing her English to (the way she speaks) her mother tongue. LIKE is followed by a noun phrase. AS (conjunction) = comparing clauses: 'She speaks English as she would speak her mother tongue' (followed by subject+verb). LIKE + noun ✓ here. Trap: 'as if' = used with a clause to suggest hypothetical comparison ('She speaks as if she were a native'); 'similar to' = grammatically awkward here.

questions.stem: The results of the experiment ______ published next month.
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Next month' indicates a future action. The passive future tense 'will be published' is correct for 'results that will be published'. WILL BE + past participle = Future Simple Passive. Trap: 'are being published' = Present Continuous Passive (suggests it's happening right now, not next month); 'has been published' = Present Perfect Passive (already completed — contradicts 'next month'); 'were published' = Simple Past Passive (already done).

questions.stem: The teacher, along with her students, ______ attending the science fair.
questions.explanation: C is correct. When the subject is connected to additional nouns by phrases like 'along with', 'together with', 'as well as', 'in addition to' — the verb agrees with the MAIN subject (before the phrase), not the added nouns. Main subject = 'The teacher' (singular) → singular verb 'is'. Trap: 'are' = treats 'teacher + students' as compound subject (wrong — 'along with' is not 'and'); 'were' = past tense, context seems present.

questions.stem: He is one of those players who ______ always given their best.
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'One of those + plural noun + who/that' takes a plural verb. The relative clause 'who ______ always given their best' refers to 'those players' (plural). The antecedent of 'who' is 'players' (plural), so the verb must be plural: 'have'. Trap: 'has' = common error where 'he' is mistaken for the antecedent (but 'who' refers to 'those players', not 'he'); 'had' = past perfect (no justification).

questions.stem: The injured were immediately ______ to the nearest hospital.
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Rushed to hospital' = the standard collocation when emergency transportation is implied (urgent, fast movement). 'Rushed to the nearest hospital' is the precise idiomatic expression in medical emergency contexts. BROUGHT = taken (doesn't carry urgency); CARRIED AWAY = idiom meaning 'to lose self-control' or 'to remove something' (wrong connotation); DRIVEN OFF = to chase away (wrong meaning entirely).

questions.stem: ______ having studied hard, she could not clear the exam.
questions.explanation: C is correct. DESPITE is a preposition followed by a noun/gerund phrase: 'Despite having studied hard'. It does NOT take a clause. Contrast: ALTHOUGH/EVEN THOUGH are conjunctions followed by a subject+verb clause: 'Although she studied hard...' Here the blank is followed by 'having studied hard' (a gerund phrase, no subject) → DESPITE is correct. Trap: 'Although/Even though' = must be followed by a subject+verb; 'However' = conjunctive adverb, doesn't connect to a participle phrase.

questions.stem: No sooner ______ the bell than the students rushed out.
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'No sooner...than' triggers inversion: 'No sooner + auxiliary + subject + verb'. Pattern: 'No sooner did + subject + V1 + than...'. 'No sooner did the bell ring than...' ✓. Note: 'ring' is correct (base form after auxiliary 'did'); 'rang' would be used WITHOUT auxiliary: 'The bell had no sooner rung than...' using 'No sooner had + subject + V3 + than'. Trap: 'did rang' = wrong — can't use both 'did' and past tense 'rang'; 'had the bell rang' = wrong past participle ('rang' is simple past; past participle of ring = 'rung').
